newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FOCUS - Kazakhs look east to China for oil markets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kazakhs look east to China for oil markets.

text.p: Kazakhstan announced a $4-billion oil deal with the Chinese National Petroleum Company (CNPC) on Wednesday, including an ambitious plan for a pipeline to its eastern neighbour, confounding sceptical western investors.

"This is very positive news as it potentially opens up a whole new market for Kazakh oil," said Charles Towers-Clark, director of research at brokers Global Kazkommerts Securities Inc in the capital of Almaty.
CNPC has promised to invest $4 billion in the Aktyubinsk oil enterprise over the next 20 years, with $585 million to be invested from 1998 to 2003, in return for a 60 percent share in the company.

In the short term, the embattled Kazakh government benefits from a $320 million bonus from CNPC, which will go some way to helping it pay off a mountainous backlog of wages and pensions owed to the 16.9 million population.
The contract also placed in check some investors' grumbles that deals have not always been solid in the former Soviet republic's roller-coaster ride to a market economy.

"The privatisations here are going very fast," a diplomat said, referring to the Kazakh government's gritty determination to sell off much of its oil and gas enterprises by July 1 in the face of strong opposition from the sector's Soviet-era managers.

Aktyubinsk is located in western Kazakhstan and has estimated oil reserves of 483 million tonnes. CNPC vice president Wu Yaowen said current annual output of crude of 2.2 million tonnes (44,000 barrels per day) would double by 2000.
But CNPC's plan to build a 3,000 km (2,000 mile) pipeline worth $3.5 billion to export the oil to the northwestern province of Xinjiang was the main reason Kazakhstan chose CNPC.
"There were some good offers from American firms," Eduard Utepov, head of the privatisation department at the Kazakh finance ministry, said in reference to tender losers Texaco Inc and Amoco Corp.
Russia's Yuzhny Most company also took part.
"But most interesting for us was the Chinese offer on oil transport," he said.
Kazakhstan's oil is caught in a web of ageing Soviet-era pipelines controlled by former colonial master Russia.
Alternative planned export routes south to the Gulf and Indian Ocean are held hostage to apparently endless fighting in Afghanistan and a United States embargo against Iran.
The export bottleneck saw the republic, a tract of barren steppe and rugged mountains the size of western Europe, achieve a lower-than-expected debt rating last year.

The contract with CNPC also sees privatisation back on the rails after a series of scrapped deals. Swiss-Swedish ABB AG Power Consortium Limited's sudden loss in May of a $1.4 billion deal to manage the republic's electricity grid rang alarm bells in the foreign investment community.
"There's a lack of business culture here," complained one western energy executive in Almaty, who's own deal is snagged. "They (Kazakhstan) don't really understand what a contract is."
